background.definition: Brain abscess is a localized, encapsulated infection of the brain parenchyma and does not include meningitis, encephalitis, or empyema of duralspaces.

list.listitem: Very uncommon diagnosis, typically 10 cases per year in a tertiary center.
In recent years, the number of abscesses from otorhinolaryngologic infection has declined while the number of abscesses in patients with compromised immunity has increased.
summarizes the nonbacterial and the bacterial causes of brain abscess.
Brain abscess affects patients of all ages and genders. About 70% of patients have at least one risk factor (see Risk Factor section).
About one-third of patients have distant sources of infection.

A bacterium, fungus, or parasite invades the brain parenchyma at a focus of ischemic necrosis by one of three pathways: contiguous spread by direct extension or venous spread from a nearby structure such as the paranasal sinus or mastoid; hematogenous spread from a distant source, most commonly the lungs or heart; or direct inoculation from trauma or surgery.
Inflammatory response involves neutrophils, astrocytes, and microglia. Later, lymphocytes, macro phages, and fibrocytes migrate to build a capsule around a necrotic center.
Surrounding edema may cause mass effect and neurologic deficits.

Counsel patients with HIV/AIDS to avoid exposure to toxoplasmosis by avoiding undercooked meats and unwashed fruits and vegetables, and washing well after gardening, cleaning litter boxes, or handling raw meat. C

list.listitem: The presentation is so variable that any combination of headache, fever, seizure, or focal neurologic deficits, behavioral changes, or decreased mental status in a patient with risk factors for brain abscess should prompt clinical suspicion.
The diagnosis is typically made about 1 week after onset of symptoms (ranges from a few hours to 2 months).
About two-thirds of patients present with headache, about half with fever or focal neurologic deficits, and about one-fourth with confusion.
Other findings consistent with increased intracranial pressure, papilledema, nausea, or vomiting occur in about half of patients.
The classic triad of headache, fever, and focal neurologic deficits is only seen in about 15% of patients.

In patients with HIV disease and new neurologic findings, the strongest single predictor of focal CT lesion is new seizuresFocal motor deficit, asymmetric deep tendon reflexes, cerebellar deficit, decreased orientation, and focal motor deficit also increase risk somewhat.
If clinically suspected, order CBC, CRP, and imaging (MRI preferred; CT if not available).
About half of patients have an elevated WBC, about two-thirds have an elevated ESR, and nearly 90% have elevated CRP.
About 20% of patients have positive blood cultures, and about one-fourth have positive CSF cultures.
Up to 13% of patients with abscess are thought to have tumor on the initial CT interpretation.

MRI with gadolinium contrast is more sensitive than CT in early abscess formation and the preferred initial study if readily available. The classic finding in CT or MRI is a ring-enhanced space-occupying lesion, and the addition of diffusion-weighted imaging to MRI assists in distinguishing tumor from abscess.
Surgical aspiration is both therapeutic and diagnostic, confirming abscess and providing gram stain/culture to guide antimicrobial therapy.
Screen HIV patients for CD4 T-lymphocyte count less than 100microliters to determine whether prophylaxis for toxoplasmosis is indicated.
Suspect brain abscess in patients with risk factors who have any combination of headache, fever, seizure, or focal neurologic deficits.
Contrast-enhanced CT is a reasonable initial study, but gadolinium-enhanced MRI is more sensitive in early brain abscess formation and is the preferred initial study if readily available.
If imaging reveals a mass lesion, obtain blood cultures, consult a neurosurgeon, and start empiric antimicrobials.
Since CSF studies are not very helpful for brain abscess, lumbar puncture is controversial especially in patients with suspected increased intracranial pressure.
Optimal treatment involves empiric antibiotics as well as surgery to debulk the infection and to obtain infected material to guide antimicrobial selection. C

Until the final culture results are available, initiate empiric antibiotics with a third-generation cephalosporin plus metronidazole to provide adequate coverage for the most common bacterial pathogens. C
When fungal elements are isolated in infected material, initiate amphotericin B, itraconazole, or voriconazole until the final pathogen is identified. C
The use of corticosteroids has not been associated with improved outcomes. B
No clinical trials exist to guide optimal therapy (eg, antimicrobial, surgery, or corticosteroids).

Antibiotics are the mainstay of treatment, and empiric antibiotics are indicated in patients for whom pathogens obtained from abscess material are identified. and summarize empiric therapy for various pathogens. Until the final culture results are available, initiate empiric antibiotics with a third-generation cephalosporin plus metronidazole to provide adequate coverage for the most common bacterial pathogens.

The duration of antibiotic therapy is typically 2 to 8 weeks parenterally,followed by 2 to 6 weeks of oral medication depending on clinical improvement. Patients who are clinically stable and demonstrate short-term improvement may be candidates for outpatient parenteral antimicrobials.

Fungal and parasitic abscesses are less common than bacterial causes and are more likely to be found in immune-compromised patients, warranting surgical confirmation of the pathogen and consideration of additional antimicrobial coverage in these patients if they fail to improve on antibiotics alone. See
Antibiotics alone are associated with favorable outcome in patients with small solitary bacterial lesions (<3 cm).

Corticosteroids are not associated with improved outcomes. They may be useful in patients with severe diffuse cerebral edema with mid line shift or with mass effects associated with progressive neurologic deterioration.
Most patients benefit from surgical intervention, typically aspiration and, less commonly, excision, as an adjunct to antimicrobial therapy.

While about 24% of patients treated with surgery plus antibiotics die compared with 45% of patients treated with antibiotics alone, this may reflect other clinical factors, including delayed diagnosis and other prognostic variables.

A Danish population-based cohort study found that the following variables were not associated with mortality risk: antibiotics before surgery, neurosurgical treatment, patient sex, and systemic corticosteroids.
All patients with evidence of brain abscess on CT or MRI require hospitalization for empiric, parenteral antibiotics and surgical consultation.
The overall mortality varies from 5% to 32%, but is as high as 86% for some parasitic and fungal abscesses. B
Higher mortality is seen in patients with fulminant course, with coma and lower Glasgow coma scale at presentation. B
Patients with hematogenous sources, multiple lesions, larger lesions, interventricular rupture, and septic shock are at higher risk of death. B
Patients with older age (>65), gram-negative bacteria, compromised immune states, and fungal or parasitic pathogens also fare poorly. B

Patients with fungal abscesses and patients who are not good surgical candidates (eg, multiple abscesses, deep or inaccessible abscesses, and comorbid critical illness) have a greater risk of death. B
About two-thirds of patients recover fully or with mild residual impairments. B
